prompt: After ana logs in to `sessions.py`, what does her client hold that the server can use to recognise her?
hint: It is meaningless on its own.

choices.text: Her name and expiry, signed with the server key
choices.why: That is what a JWT holds. In a session the claims stay on the server, in the row.

choices.text: A random id
choices.why: Right. The id is a key to a row the server keeps; it carries no information of its own.

choices.text: A hash of her password, so she need not type it again
choices.why: A password hash never leaves the server. Sending one would make the hash itself a password.

choices.text: A copy of her row from the sessions table
choices.why: The row stays on the server; the client gets only the id that finds it, and the table even stores that id hashed.

prompt: A colleague says the team moved from session cookies to JWTs "because cookies are less secure". What does this lesson say the move actually changed?
hint: Both are presented on every request.

choices.text: Where the login state lives
choices.why: Right. A session keeps it in a row on the server; a token carries it, signed. Neither is secure or insecure by kind.

choices.text: It removed the bearer secret: a JWT proves identity in itself, so nothing can be stolen
choices.why: A JWT is a bearer credential too: whoever presents it is treated as its owner, exactly like a session id.

choices.text: It moved HTTPS from optional to required
choices.why: Both need HTTPS for the same reason: anyone who reads either one on the wire can use it.

choices.text: It moved the credential from a cookie into a header
choices.why: That is the carrier, and it is independent of the choice: a JWT can travel in a cookie and a session id in a header.

prompt: Match each job to how it is done when nothing extra is added to either model.
hint: One model looks up, the other computes.

pairs.right: look the id up in a table
recompute the signature with the key

right_distractors: ask the browser to delete its copy

prompt: Match each attribute of `sessions.py`'s `Set-Cookie` to what it tells the client.
hint: None of them is sent back to the server.

pairs.right: never show it to the page's scripts
leave it off requests other sites start, apart from following a link
forget it after half an hour

right_distractors: send it to every subdomain as well

prompt: The `sessions` table stores `id_hash`, the SHA-256 of the cookie's value, and not the value itself. What does that protect against?
hint: Think of who might read the database without being the server.

choices.text: A stolen cookie being used from another machine
choices.why: A stolen cookie still works: the server hashes what it receives and finds the row. The hash protects the table, not the cookie.

choices.text: Someone guessing a valid id
choices.why: The 32 random bytes are what make guessing hopeless; hashing them adds nothing there.

choices.text: A leaked copy of the database, such as a forgotten backup, giving its reader working cookies
choices.why: Right. The reader gets hashes, and a hash cannot be turned back into an id the server would accept.

choices.text: The cookie expiring before the row does
choices.why: Expiry is the `expires` column and `Max-Age`; the hash has nothing to do with time.

prompt: `sessions.py` answered a login with `Set-Cookie: sid=…; Path=/; Max-Age=1800; …`. After how many minutes does a well-behaved client drop the cookie?
hint: `Max-Age` counts seconds.

prompt: The login to `shop.test`, a name `--resolve` pointed at the same server, received `Set-Cookie: sid=…; Secure; …`, and curl's jar stayed empty. Why?
hint: The same server gave localhost a cookie curl kept.

choices.text: It arrived over plain HTTP to a host that is not localhost
choices.why: Right. curl, like browsers, counts localhost as secure; `shop.test` over `http://` is not.

choices.text: `HttpOnly` hides the cookie from programs such as curl, which are not browsers
choices.why: `HttpOnly` hides a cookie from a page's JavaScript. curl stored the localhost cookie with the same flag.

choices.text: `SameSite=Lax` blocks cookies for a host name the client has never visited before
choices.why: SameSite is about requests other sites start. This was a direct login, and curl does not apply SameSite anyway.

choices.text: The server only sets cookies for requests addressed to localhost
choices.why: The `Set-Cookie` header is in the answer. The server sent it; the client chose not to keep it.

prompt: After the logout, `kept.txt` still held ana's old `sid`, and `/me` answered `sign in first`. What made the copy useless?
hint: Look at the table, not at the jar.

choices.text: `Max-Age=0` in the logout answer
choices.why: `Max-Age=0` asks a client to drop its cookie. `kept.txt` was never told and kept it; the refusal came from elsewhere.

choices.text: The missing CSRF token
choices.why: `/me` is a GET and needs no CSRF token. It refused because no live session matched.

choices.text: curl deleting the cookie from its jar
choices.why: curl emptied `jar.txt`, not the copy. Deleting a client's cookie is housekeeping; the copy shows it.

choices.text: The server deleted the row
choices.why: Right. With the row gone the id is a key to nothing, wherever copies of it are.

prompt: Put the logout in `sessions.py` in the order it happens.
hint: The server acts before it answers.
items: The client sends `POST /logout` with the cookie and `X-CSRF-Token`
The server finds the session by the hash of the cookie
The client drops the cookie from its jar
trap: Dropping the cookie comes last and matters least: the row was already gone.

prompt: Bruno changes his password because he thinks someone else has been signing in as him. With sessions stored as rows, what should the server do?
hint: The other person may already be signed in.

choices.text: Nothing more: every session expires within thirty minutes anyway
choices.why: Thirty minutes is a long time for an intruder, and a session can be renewed. The fix is available now, so use it.

choices.text: Delete every session of his except the one he is using
choices.why: Right. The intruder's session is one of those rows; deleting it signs them out at once.

choices.text: Send `Max-Age=0` in the answer to the password change
choices.why: That reaches only Bruno's own browser, and it would log him out while leaving the intruder signed in.

choices.text: Delete only the session he changed the password from
choices.why: That is the one session known to be his. The intruder's rows would survive untouched.

prompt: A page on another site cannot read shelf's answers. Why can it still harm ana's account through CSRF?
hint: What does the browser add without asking?

choices.text: It can read ana's cookie with JavaScript and send it to itself
choices.why: A page cannot read another site's cookies at all, and `HttpOnly` hides them even from shelf's own pages. CSRF needs no reading.

choices.text: The same-origin policy does not apply to forms
choices.why: It does: the page still cannot read the answer. The harm happens without reading it.

choices.text: Cookies with `Secure` are sent to every site
choices.why: `Secure` restricts a cookie to HTTPS; it never widens where it goes.

choices.text: The browser attaches ana's cookie, and the request does its work before any answer
choices.why: Right. Adding a book or changing an address is done by the time the answer arrives; reading it is unnecessary.

prompt: The cookie attribute `SameSite=___` leaves the cookie off a `POST` that another site starts, but still sends it when the user follows a link.
hint: Not the strictest of the three values.

prompt: Which of these, set in `sessions.py`, can stop a forged `POST /wishlist` started by another site's page? Choose all that apply.
hint: One works in the browser, one in the server.

choices.text: `SameSite=Lax` on the cookie
choices.why: Right. The browser sends that cross-site POST without the cookie, so the server sees a stranger.

choices.text: The `X-CSRF-Token` check
choices.why: Right. The other page cannot read the token and a form cannot set the header, so the request gets 403.

choices.text: `HttpOnly` on the cookie
choices.why: `HttpOnly` keeps scripts from reading the cookie. The forged request never reads it; the browser attaches it.

choices.text: Storing the session id as a hash
choices.why: The hash protects a copy of the table. A forged request carries the real cookie, which hashes to the real row.

prompt: Who can read the payload of the access token `tokens.py` issued to ana?
hint: `basenc` read it without any key.

choices.text: Only a server holding `jwt.key`
choices.why: The key is needed to sign, and to check a signature. Reading the payload is decoding base64url, which needs nothing.

choices.text: Nobody: the payload is encrypted
choices.why: A signed JWT is encoded, not encrypted. The encrypted format, JWE, is a different thing and rarely used.

choices.text: Anyone holding the token
choices.why: Right. That is why a payload carries identifiers and times, never secrets.

choices.text: Only ana and shelf, named in `sub` and `aud`
choices.why: Claims say who the token is about and for; they do not restrict who can decode it.

prompt: The payload part of ana's token was 159 characters of base64url, with the padding dropped. How many `=` must be added before a strict decoder accepts it?
hint: Base64 works in groups of four characters.

prompt: `basenc --base64url -d` printed the whole payload and then `basenc: invalid input`. What was it complaining about?
hint: The JSON came out complete.

choices.text: The characters `-` and `_`, which base64 does not use
choices.why: Plain `base64` would object to those, but `--base64url` is the alphabet that has them. The complaint was at the end.

choices.text: The signature, which is not valid base64url
choices.why: `cut -d. -f2` passed only the payload; the signature never reached the decoder.

choices.text: A payload encrypted with `jwt.key`, which `basenc` cannot open
choices.why: If it were encrypted, the JSON would not have appeared. It was readable because it is only encoded.

choices.text: The missing `=` padding at the end
choices.why: Right. JWTs drop it, so a part whose length is not a multiple of four looks cut short.

prompt: `sed` changed one letter so the payload said `"sub":"2"`, and kept the old signature. Why could whoever made that edit not simply fix the signature too?
hint: `hs256.py` computed it in five lines.

choices.text: The signature is encrypted
choices.why: It is an HMAC written in base64url; anyone can read it, and reading it reveals nothing about the key.

choices.text: The server keeps a copy of every signature it issued and compares
choices.why: Nothing is stored at issue. The server recomputes the signature from the token and the key on every request.

choices.text: Computing it needs the 32 bytes in `jwt.key`
choices.why: Right. With the key anyone can sign anything, which is why the key is the secret and the signature is not.

choices.text: Base64url cannot encode a changed payload of the same length
choices.why: It encoded it fine; `cut` and `basenc` read `"sub":"2"` back out of the edited token.

prompt: Put the steps of verifying an HS256 token by hand, as `hs256.py` does, in order.
hint: The signature is computed over the text as it appears in the token.
items: Split the token at its two dots
Join header and payload with the dot, exactly as written
Compute HMAC-SHA256 of that text with the key
Write the result in base64url without padding
Compare it with the third part using `compare_digest`
trap: Decoding the payload is not a step: the HMAC is computed over the encoded text.

prompt: Ten internal services verify HS256 tokens, so each holds the same key. One of them is breached and its configuration leaks. What can the attacker now do?
hint: What else does the key that verifies do?

choices.text: Read the payloads of every token, which were unreadable before the leak
choices.why: Payloads were always readable; that needs no key.

choices.text: Mint tokens for any user that all ten services accept
choices.why: Right. With HS256 the key that verifies also signs. RS256 or ES256 would have given each service only a public key, which cannot sign.

choices.text: Forge tokens accepted by the breached service only
choices.why: The key is the same everywhere, so a token it signs is good everywhere.

choices.text: Nothing lasting: tokens expire in five minutes
choices.why: Short lifetimes limit a stolen token. A stolen key lets the attacker mint a fresh token whenever one expires.

prompt: Match each registered claim to what it says.
hint: Seven names, three letters each.

prompt: `tokens.issue(1, now=time.time() - 310)` made a token whose lifetime is 300 seconds, and `/me` accepted it. Why?
hint: Look at what `verify` passes besides the key.

choices.text: It expired ten seconds earlier, within the thirty seconds of leeway
choices.why: Right. Leeway forgives small clock differences between machines; at 600 seconds the same call was refused.

choices.text: PyJWT does not check `exp` unless asked
choices.why: It checks `exp` whenever the token has one, and the 600-second token was refused for it.

choices.text: `nbf` was set, and that overrides `exp`
choices.why: `nbf` is the earliest moment a token is valid. It has no say over when it stops.

choices.text: Tokens made by importing `tokens.py` skip the checks
choices.why: Importing gives the same `issue` the server uses, and the server checked this token as it checks any other.

prompt: `tokens.py` gives an access token 300 seconds and verifies with `leeway=30`. About how many seconds after a token was issued does `/me` start refusing it as expired?
hint: The leeway is added on top of the lifetime.

prompt: A token whose header says `"alg": "none"` and whose third part is empty reached `/me`. Which argument in `verify` made the API refuse it?
hint: The refusal said `The specified alg value is not allowed`.

choices.text: `audience=AUDIENCE`
choices.why: The token even carried `"aud": "shelf-api"`. It was refused before any claim was read.

choices.text: `options={"require": [...]}`
choices.why: The token did lack `exp`, but the algorithm check comes first, and the message names the algorithm.

choices.text: `leeway=LEEWAY`
choices.why: Leeway only stretches the time checks; it has nothing to say about how a token is signed.

choices.text: `algorithms=["HS256"]`
choices.why: Right. The server, not the token, decides how a token must be signed, and `none` is not on its list.

prompt: The login's refresh token was presented a second time, and `tokens.py` deleted the whole family. What still worked afterwards?
hint: Which of them was never stored?

choices.text: The second refresh token, issued before the reuse
choices.why: It was in the family and was deleted with it: `unknown or expired refresh token`.

choices.text: Nothing at all: the whole sign-in was revoked
choices.why: Every refresh token was, but `/me` still answered ana with the access token already issued.

choices.text: The access token from the first refresh, until its `exp`
choices.why: Right. Nothing about it was stored, so there was nothing to delete. Only its expiry ends it.

choices.text: The first refresh token, for whoever presented it first
choices.why: It had been spent at the first refresh; the second presentation is what revealed the copy.

prompt: `logout` in `tokens.py` deletes denylist rows whose `exp` has passed. Why is it safe to forget those revoked tokens?
hint: What would happen to such a token without the denylist?

choices.text: Past its `exp`, the token is refused anyway
choices.why: Right. The denylist only has to cover the window between revocation and expiry, which is what keeps it small.

choices.text: A revoked token's refresh token is deleted too, so it cannot come back
choices.why: Refreshing makes a new access token with a new `jti`; it never brings an old one back. The old one could still be replayed until its `exp`.

choices.text: The client has thrown it away by then
choices.why: What a client does is not something the server can rely on; a copy elsewhere is the whole reason for the denylist.

choices.text: `jti` values are reused after the token expires
choices.why: They are 16 random hex digits, drawn fresh for every token.

prompt: A team wants JWT logout to take effect immediately and also wants no lookup of any kind on each request. What can they have?
hint: Immediate means the server remembers the logout.

choices.text: Both, with refresh token rotation on every sign-out
choices.why: Rotation protects refresh tokens. The access token already issued stays valid until `exp`, as `/me` showed.

choices.text: Both, by setting `exp` to the moment the user logs out of the application
choices.why: `exp` is inside a token already signed and in the client's hands; changing it would break the signature.

choices.text: Only one: revoking early needs state that the server checks every time
choices.why: Right. Without a lookup the best they get is a short lifetime, which bounds the delay without removing it.

choices.text: Both, by deleting the token from the client's storage as it logs out
choices.why: That removes one copy. Any other copy is still signed and still unexpired.

prompt: An attacker manages to run a script inside shelf's page. What changes if the credential is in an `HttpOnly` cookie instead of `localStorage`?
hint: Both cases are bad; one is bounded.

choices.text: It acts while the tab is open, and cannot carry the credential off
choices.why: Right. From `localStorage` it could copy the token and use it from another machine until it expired.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because the script runs on the same origin as the page
choices.why: Same origin means the script can read `localStorage`. It still cannot read an `HttpOnly` cookie.

choices.text: The script can no longer make requests as the user
choices.why: It can, while the page is open: the browser attaches the cookie to its requests.

choices.text: CSRF stops being possible
choices.why: The other way round: a cookie is attached automatically, which is exactly what CSRF needs.

prompt: Why should a token never be put in a URL, such as `/me?token=eyJ…`?
hint: Think of where addresses end up.

choices.text: URLs cannot hold a dot
choices.why: They can, and base64url was chosen so that a token is safe in one. The problem is where URLs are copied.

choices.text: Logs, history and the `Referer` header keep addresses, and none of them is secret
choices.why: Right. A bearer credential written into any of them works for whoever reads it.

choices.text: The server cannot verify a signature that arrives in a query string instead of a header
choices.why: It could read and verify it from anywhere. Where it is visible to others is the issue.

choices.text: A query string is sent only with `GET`
choices.why: A query string can go with any method; that is not the risk.

prompt: A team builds a web application whose pages call only its own API, on the same host. Which does this lesson recommend as the starting point?
hint: A browser talking to its own API.

choices.text: JWTs kept in `localStorage` and sent in the `Authorization` header on each call
choices.why: That trades CSRF for exposure to any injected script, and revocation gets harder. Nothing here crosses a boundary.

choices.text: A session cookie with `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite`, plus a CSRF token
choices.why: Right. Revoked by deleting a row, nothing readable in the browser, and the lookup is cheap.

choices.text: OAuth 2.0 with an external provider
choices.why: That is for signing in with somebody else's accounts or acting on a user's behalf, lesson 9; it is not a default for an app's own login.

choices.text: API keys, one per user
choices.why: API keys identify programs, as lesson 7 showed; a person in a browser logs in.

prompt: Ana's session id was 43 characters and her access token 240. How many more characters does the token add to every request?
hint: A subtraction.

prompt: An orders service has to know which user sent each request, and the team does not want it to call the login service on every request. What fits best?
hint: The request crosses a boundary between services.

choices.text: Share the session table with the orders service
choices.why: That is a lookup on every request by another name, and it ties the two services to one database.

choices.text: Forward the user's password with each request
choices.why: Every service would then hold passwords, the worst thing to spread around.

choices.text: Send the session cookie to the orders service
choices.why: It would still have to ask the login service what the id means.

choices.text: A short-lived signed token it verifies with a public key
choices.why: Right. The orders service checks the signature alone, and with RS256 or ES256 it cannot mint tokens itself.

prompt: Which of these take effect at once, so that a copy of the credential made earlier stops working on the next request? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ask, for each, whether the server keeps a record it checks.

choices.text: Deleting the session's row in `sessions.py`
choices.why: Right. The next lookup finds nothing, whoever sends the id.

choices.text: Putting the token's `jti` on the denylist that `verify` reads
choices.why: Right. `token revoked` came back on the very next request.

choices.text: Sending `Max-Age=0` for the session cookie
choices.why: That asks one client to drop its cookie; `kept.txt` shows a copy surviving it.

choices.text: Rotating the refresh token after a reuse
choices.why: The refresh family dies, and the access token already issued keeps working until its `exp`.

prompt: A team moves its JWT from `localStorage` into an `HttpOnly` cookie, so that its pages' scripts cannot read it. Which defence from this lesson does the token now need that it did not need before?
hint: What does a browser do with a cookie that it never did with a header?

choices.text: Pinning `algorithms=["HS256"]`
choices.why: That was needed all along, wherever the token travels.

choices.text: Hashing the token before storing it
choices.why: The server stores nothing of an access token; there is no table to protect.

choices.text: `SameSite` and a CSRF token
choices.why: Right. A cookie is attached automatically, so another site can make the browser send it. In a header, page code had to add it.

choices.text: A shorter `exp`, because cookies are easier to steal
choices.why: An `HttpOnly` cookie is harder for a script to steal than `localStorage`; the new exposure is forged requests, not theft.

prompt: Both `sessions.py` and `tokens.py` store each random token they hand out only as its SHA-256 ___, so a copy of `shelf.db` contains nothing a client could present.
hint: The column is called `id_hash`.
